Mr. Woodhouse agreed with everything, but added,

“Our young friend Harriet Smith, though, is another very pretty, pleasant girl. You will like Harriet. Emma could not find a better companion than Harriet.”

“I am delighted to hear it—but Jane Fairfax is known to be so talented and exceptional! And she is exactly Emma’s age.”

They discussed this subject very happily, then moved on to others of similar importance, all with the same friendly agreement. Yet the evening did not end without a little renewed distress. When the gruel arrived, it gave them plenty to discuss. They praised it, offered many comments, and agreed without question that it was healthy for everyone. They also spoke quite harshly of the many households where it was never served in an acceptable state. Unfortunately, the most recent failure Mr. Woodhouse’s daughter could mention, and therefore the one she spoke of most, concerned her own cook at South End. This young woman, hired for their stay, had never understood what she meant by a bowl of nice, smooth gruel, thin but not too thin. However often she had wanted it and ordered it, she had never received anything tolerable. This opened a dangerous subject.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and looking at her with loving concern. To Emma, that little cry meant, “Ah! There is no end to the sad results of your going to South End. I cannot bear to talk about it.” For a little while she hoped he really would not talk about it, and that some silent reflection would be enough to let him enjoy his own smooth gruel again. After several minutes, however, he began:

“I shall always regret that you went to the seaside this autumn instead of coming here.”

“But why should you regret it, sir? I assure you, it did the children a great deal of good.”

“And besides, if you had to visit the sea, you should have gone somewhere other than South End. South End is unhealthy. Perry was surprised to hear you had chosen it.”

“I know many people think that, but they are quite mistaken, sir. We were all perfectly healthy there and never suffered the slightest inconvenience from the mud. Mr. Wingfield says it is entirely wrong to think the place unhealthy. I am sure we can trust him: he thoroughly understands the qualities of the air, and his own brother and family have stayed there many times.”

“You should have gone to Cromer, my dear, if you went anywhere. Perry once spent a week at Cromer, and he considers it the best of all the places for sea bathing.

All these things, and others—many others—I would gladly describe at length. But, briefly, I must receive my recompense. I long to return to my family and my house; and in exchange for any further intelligence I may impart—in view of the illumination I can offer upon numerous highly important departments of physical and metaphysical science—I must beg the influence of your honorable body to secure a pardon for my crime in causing the deaths of the creditors when I left Rotterdam. Such, then, is the purpose of this document. The bearer, a dweller upon the moon whom I have persuaded, and duly instructed, to serve as my messenger to earth, will wait upon your Excellencies’ decision and bring back the desired pardon, should it prove possible by any means to obtain one.

“I have the honor to remain, etc., your Excellencies’ most humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

Having completed his reading of this exceedingly remarkable paper, Professor Rub-a-dub is reported to have let his pipe fall to the ground from sheer amazement. Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, meanwhile, removed his spectacles, polished them, and put them into his pocket; then, forgetting alike his dignity and himself, he spun three times upon his heel in a very ecstasy of wonder and admiration. There could be no question: the pardon must be secured. This, at any rate, Professor Rub-a-dub declared with a hearty oath, and the celebrated Von Underduk ultimately reached the same conclusion. Taking his fellow scientist’s arm, he set off homeward without a word, to consider what steps they should take. At the burgomaster’s door, however, the professor ventured to observe that the messenger had chosen to vanish—doubtless terrified out of his wits by the ferocious appearance of Rotterdam’s burghers. A pardon would consequently serve little purpose, since nobody but a lunar inhabitant would attempt a journey over such an immense distance. The burgomaster acknowledged the justice of this remark, and there the affair ended. Rumour and conjecture, however, did not end with it. Publication of the letter occasioned a great diversity of gossip and opinion. Certain persons of excessive wisdom even exposed themselves to ridicule by denouncing the entire affair as a mere hoax. With people of this description, however, hoax is, I believe, a comprehensive name for anything beyond their understanding. As for myself, I cannot imagine what evidence supports their charge. Let us examine their assertions:

“Well, Jup,” I said, “what’s wrong now? How is your master?”

“Well, to tell the truth, sir, he’s not as well as he could be.”

“Not well! I’m very sorry to hear that. What symptoms does he complain of?”

“There! That’s the trouble! He never complains about anything, but he’s very sick all the same.”

“Very sick, Jupiter! Why didn’t you say so straight away? Is he confined to bed?”

“No, he isn’t! He isn’t confined anywhere—that’s just the problem. I’ve been worrying myself sick about poor Master Will.”

“Jupiter, I’d like to understand what you’re talking about. You say your master is ill. Hasn’t he told you what’s wrong with him?”

“Well, sir, there’s no point getting angry over it. Master Will says there’s nothing wrong with him at all—but then why does he go around looking like this, his head down and his shoulders up, and white as a ghost? And he keeps on ciphering all the time—”

“Keeps on doing what, Jupiter?”

“Ciphering, with figures on the slate—the strangest figures I ever saw. I’m getting scared, I tell you. I have to keep a very close watch on what he gets up to. The other day he slipped away from me before sunrise and stayed out the whole blessed day. I’d cut a big stick ready to give him a damned good beating when he came back—but I’m such a fool I couldn’t bring myself to do it in the end. He looked so poorly.”

“Eh? What? Ah, yes! All things considered, I think you’d better not be too hard on the poor fellow. Don’t beat him, Jupiter—he’s hardly in a state to bear it. But have you any idea what caused this illness, or rather, this change in his behaviour? Has anything upsetting happened since I saw you?”

“No, sir, nothing upsetting has happened since then. I’m afraid it was before that—on the very day you were there.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“Why, sir, I mean that bug. There it is.”

“The what?”

“The bug. I’m certain that gold-bug bit Master Will somewhere on his head.”

“And what cause have you, Jupiter, to think that?”

“Claws enough, sir, and a mouth too. I never saw such a devil of a bug. It kicks and bites anything that gets near it. Master Will caught it first, but he had to let go again pretty quickly, I can tell you—that must have been when it bit him. I didn’t like the look of its mouth myself, no way, so I wouldn’t pick it up with my fingers. I caught it in a piece of paper I found.
